passage:
Tanuja was five, and the red drum was hers. Chetan, the neighbour's boy, wanted it. Tanuja's mother said, "Give Chetan a turn, please."
Tanuja held the drum to her chest, looked at her mother's face, and slowly held it out. Her lower lip pushed forward. She put her hands behind her back.
Chetan banged it three times and grinned. Tanuja watched his hands, not his face, then went to the bookshelf and pulled at a corner of the rug.
Her mother knelt beside her. "That was hard, wasn't it?" Tanuja nodded. "It's still yours. He'll give it back."

qa.q: What toy did Tanuja hand to Chetan?
qa.a: She handed him her red drum.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling as she handed over the drum?
qa.a: She was sad and reluctant. Her pushed-out lip, her hands hidden behind her back and her walking off to pull at the rug show it cost her.

qa.q: How could Tanuja's mother help after the turn began?
qa.a: She could name the feeling, as she did, and remind Tanuja that the drum is still hers and will come back. She could also offer a choice of when the turn ends.

qa.q: How might Chetan have seen the drum being handed over?
qa.a: Chetan likely saw only the good part, a toy to bang. He may not have noticed how hard it was for Tanuja to let go.

grounding: A child hands over a toy after a parent's urging but feels the loss strongly.

passage:
Leela sat on the balcony floor with her sticker book. The neighbour's boy watched through the railing.
"Leela, would you show him one sticker?" Papa asked. His name was Samir.
"No."
"He likes the fish."
"They're MY fish."
"I know. What if he holds the book for a minute and you stay next to him?"
Leela hugged the book. Then, slowly: "Only the fish page."
She turned it, kept hold of one corner, and said, "Careful."
Afterwards she climbed onto Papa's lap. "I didn't like it," she whispered.
"Thank you for telling me. You can say no another time too."

qa.q: Which page of the sticker book did Leela agree to show?
qa.a: She agreed to show only the fish page.

qa.q: What is Leela feeling when she whispers that she didn't like it?
qa.a: She feels upset and a bit worried that giving up the book was wrong. She holds a corner and tells her papa honestly how she felt.

qa.q: What did Samir do that helped Leela stay honest about her feelings?
qa.a: He suggested she stay next to the boy and then thanked her for telling him how she felt. He also told her she could say no another time.

qa.q: What might Samir have been hoping for when he asked Leela to show one sticker?
qa.a: He probably hoped she would learn to share kindly. He offered ways for her to keep control, so he also seems to want her to feel safe saying no.

grounding: A child shares her stickers after a parent's urging yet feels the loss, and says so.

passage: At the park in Dublin, Liam was filling his yellow digger with sand. A little girl, Nour, stood close, watching. "Liam, let Nour have a turn," said Mum. Liam held the digger tight. "Mine." "Just a short turn, love. Sharing is kind." Slowly, Liam opened his hands. Nour grabbed it and ran to the slide. Liam's lip wobbled. He sat very still in the sand, staring after his digger, fists pressed into his knees. Mum knelt and rubbed his back. "That was hard, wasn't it?" He nodded and leaned into her.

qa.q: What colour was Liam's digger?
qa.a: It was yellow.

qa.q: How can you tell Liam felt sad after giving Nour the digger?
qa.a: His lip wobbled, he sat very still staring after it with his fists pressed into his knees, and he leaned into Mum.

qa.q: What did Mum do well after Liam shared?
qa.a: She knelt, rubbed his back and named that it was hard, so Liam's feeling of loss was noticed and not brushed aside.

qa.q: What would change if Liam had chosen to share on his own?
qa.a: He might have felt proud instead of only losing something, and the sharing would have been his own gift rather than an instruction.

grounding: Shows a young child handing over a toy after a parent urges it and feeling the loss sharply.

passage: The clinic waiting room was full. Zubin, five, zoomed his little red car along the bench. Beside them, a boy named Arnab was crying and pointing at the car. "Zubin, beta, give it to him for a bit," Papa said. "He's poorly." Zubin looked at Papa, then at the car. Papa nodded again. Zubin held it out without looking. Arnab stopped crying at once. Zubin climbed into Papa's lap, pressed his face against Papa's shirt, and stayed there, very quiet, peeking at his car every few seconds.

qa.q: Where were Zubin and Papa waiting?
qa.a: In the clinic waiting room.

qa.q: What does Zubin peeking at his car every few seconds suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Zubin still missed his car and felt a little sad, even though he had handed it over.

qa.q: How could Papa support Zubin after this?
qa.a: Papa could hug him and say, 'That was hard, and it helped Arnab,' and make sure the car comes back before they leave.

qa.q: How might Arnab's family see Zubin's action?
qa.a: They were probably relieved and grateful that the crying stopped in a crowded waiting room.

grounding: Shows a young child giving up a toy at a parent's urging while clearly feeling the loss.

passage:
Monday: Cousin Raghav came to visit. Mama said, "Kamal, share your spinning top." Kamal handed it over and then cried in the corner till Raghav left.
Wednesday: Raghav came again. Kamal hid the top under his pillow before the doorbell stopped ringing.
Saturday: Kamal watched Papa hold his big umbrella over the neighbour at the gate. Later, when Raghav visited, Kamal took out the top. He held it for a long moment. Then he gave it to Raghav, all by himself. He watched it spin, a little worried, and clapped when it wobbled back.

qa.q: Where did Kamal hide the top on Wednesday?
qa.a: Under his pillow.

qa.q: How was Kamal feeling on Saturday when he held the top for a long moment?
qa.a: He felt a little worried and unsure about letting go, but chose to share it anyway.

qa.q: What could Mama try next time instead of telling Kamal to share?
qa.a: She could let Kamal decide, maybe asking, 'Would you like to give Raghav a turn?' and praising him when he chooses to.

qa.q: What changed between Monday and Saturday for Raghav?
qa.a: On Monday Raghav got the top from an order and Kamal cried; on Saturday he got it as a gift and Kamal clapped with him.

grounding: Shows a child moving from forced sharing, felt as loss, to sharing on his own after copying his father's kindness.

passage: The night train was hot and crowded, and the baby across the aisle, Jatin, had been crying since Kota. He kept reaching for Rekha's tin bird. "Rekha, let him hold it for a little while," Mummy said. Rekha squeezed the bird. "It's mine." "Just till he sleeps. Please, beta." Rekha held it out slowly, her fingers opening one at a time. Jatin stopped crying at once. Rekha did not. She pushed her face into Mummy's dupatta and peeked at the bird over her arm the whole time, counting its wings.

qa.q: What toy did Rekha give to Jatin?
qa.a: She gave him her tin bird.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel after handing over the bird?
qa.a: She felt sad and anxious about her toy 🥺, hiding her face in Mummy's dupatta and watching the bird the whole time.

qa.q: What could Mummy do to help Rekha with this kind of sharing?
qa.a: Mummy could thank Rekha, say that it was hard, and make sure the bird comes back when Jatin sleeps, so sharing feels safe next time.

qa.q: What would change if Rekha had chosen to share without being asked?
qa.a: Giving the bird would have felt like her own kind choice, so she might feel warm about it instead of only feeling the loss.

grounding: Shows a young child handing over a toy on a crowded train after a parent's urging while still feeling the loss keenly.
